pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Pick three OWASP Top 10 categories and describe, for each, a concrete code pattern that has that vulnerability.
expected_points: injection: untrusted text concatenated into SQL/shell/HTML that an engine parses
broken access control: authenticated but unauthorized reach, e.g. incrementing an id or ../ path traversal
cryptographic failures: plaintext or fast-hashed passwords, hardcoded secrets, homemade crypto
any other category with a matching concrete pattern (SSRF: server fetches user-supplied URL; misconfiguration: default creds/debug endpoints; outdated components: dependency with a known CVE)

questions.prompt: What is a trust boundary, where was it in the vault exercise, and why validate with an allowlist instead of a blocklist?
expected_points: the line where data from outside your control enters code that acts on it (args, env, files, network, db content)
in vault: the exported functions receiving caller-supplied names/paths/passwords
blocklists fail open — attackers find the character you forgot; allowlists fail closed by accepting only the known-safe shape
validate at the boundary so interior code can trust its inputs

questions.prompt: Explain what `nobody' OR '1'='1` does to a concatenated SQL query, and why a parameterized query stops it where escaping quotes would not.
expected_points: concatenation lets the payload's quote terminate the string so OR '1'='1' becomes SQL that matches every row
parameterization sends query text and values in separate channels; the value is bound as data and never parsed as SQL
escaping is a blocklist with dialect/encoding corner cases — fragile by construction

questions.prompt: Why must secrets never be committed to source control, and what is the correct handling — including after one has already leaked?
expected_points: a commit lives in history forever, in every clone/fork/backup; deleting it later removes nothing
read secrets at runtime from environment variables or a secret store; local dev uses untracked files
missing secret should be a loud startup error, never a baked-in fallback
a leaked secret is revoked and rotated, not just removed from the code

questions.prompt: Why is SHA-256 the wrong way to store passwords, and what do bcrypt's salt and work factor each buy you?
expected_points: SHA-256 is deliberately fast, so stolen hashes fall to offline GPU guessing at billions per second
unsalted equal passwords share a hash — rainbow tables and cross-user cracking
salt: random per password, defeats precomputation and hash clustering
work factor: tunable slowness that keeps guessing expensive as hardware improves; both stored inside the hash string

questions.prompt: Your teammate fixes ReadNote by rejecting any name containing `..`. Is that enough? What would you do instead?
expected_points: no — absolute paths bypass it, and it wrongly rejects harmless names like notes..txt
allowlist the shape instead: filepath.IsLocal (or os.Root) guarantees the resolved path stays inside the directory

questions.prompt: Why does generating a session token with math/rand instead of crypto/rand matter, and why do secret comparisons use constant-time functions?
expected_points: math/rand is predictable — an attacker can reconstruct the sequence and mint valid tokens; crypto/rand draws from the OS CSPRNG
variable-time comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched, enabling byte-by-byte timing attacks; constant-time compare gives no signal
